/usr/local/bin/jigc
The `jigc` CLI — a context compiler for coding agents

Usage: jigc [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  start           Start or resume work. Bare `jigc start` orients (read-only); an `<intent>` composes the cascade's `default-workflow` — shipped as the `router`, a `creates-task: false` selection pass that routes the intent to a work-workflow and mints **nothing**; `jigc start --workflow <X> "<intent>"` composes `<X>` and mints the task iff `<X>` declares `creates-task: true`; `--task <id>` resumes an existing task and re-composes it
  workflow        Re-enter a milestone sub-task, or preview a work-minting workflow — compose the named `<W>`. `--task <id>` re-enters the sub-task `<id>` as a fanned sub-agent (`<W>` must equal the sub-task's recorded mint workflow, else rejected — distinct from `jigc start --task`, which recomposes a top-level task's own workflow). `--preview` composes a `creates-task: true` `<W>` **without minting a task**, so an agent can read what it will ask before consenting to mint. Exactly one of the two is required
  doc             Read and write managed docs — the `jigc doc <verb>` surface
  task            The task lifecycle surface — `jigc task <verb> <id>` over a named task's working area
  config          The cascade surface — `jigc config <verb>` reads what the knobs currently resolve to (`get` / `list`) and records deltas into the project layer (`.jigc/config/`)
  milestone       The milestone work-unit surface — `jigc milestone <verb>` mints a milestone, builds its sub-task list, and executes, joins, and finalizes it — or, when the work is abandoned, discards it
  setup           Install the Claude Code adapter — writes the `.jigc/AGENT.md` bootstrap and a reference into `CLAUDE.md`, initializes the project layer (`.jigc/config/`), allowlists `Bash(jigc:*)`, and installs the `SessionStart` and warn-only git `pre-commit` hooks. Idempotent
  uninstall       Reverse this project's jigc install — removes `.jigc/`, unwires the `CLAUDE.md` reference, and drops the `Bash(jigc:*)` permit from `.claude/settings.json`. Leaves the machine-global `doc-code` probe (shared across repos) in place. Idempotent: a second run is a clean no-op, and the host files it edits (`CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, a wrapped `pre-commit` hook) keep your own content byte-for-byte. Three states it refuses instead of destroying, because `.jigc/` is their only copy — a fan-out sub-task path under `.jigc/worktrees/` that holds content blocks with `uninstall.dirty-worktree` (get the work out — or, for a path this repository has registered as a worktree, abandon the milestone with `jigc milestone discard <milestone-id> --force`), an open task under `.jigc/tasks/` holding a staged doc no commit has a copy of blocks with `uninstall.staged-prose` (throw the task away with `jigc task discard <task-id> --force`, or land it with `jigc task finalize <task-id>` once its doc is complete), and any other file under `.jigc/` that no index has a copy of — a recorded config delta among them — blocks with `uninstall.untracked-workbench-file` (`git add <path>` is enough to make it recoverable). Any of them removes nothing until you re-run — or pass `--force`, which deletes all three with the install
  upgrade         Re-check every recorded config delta against the current pack and report what needs attention. Report-and-route only — it changes nothing, and exits non-zero if any finding blocks
  ingest          Scan the project for existing markdown docs, adopt every conformant one (register-only — never moving or rewriting a file), and print a triage report. Misplaced or non-conformant files are flagged for a human; exits 0. A flagged non-conformant file is rewritten into managed shape with `jigc migrate <path> --as <doctype>`
  migrate         Rewrite a foreign, non-conformant document into managed shape — `jigc migrate <path> --as <doctype>`. Mints a migration task and composes the `migrate-<doctype>` workflow so the agent re-authors the content through the write verbs. Works for any doctype with a shipped `migrate-<doctype>` workflow — see the error message for the live set. An already-conformant file needs no rewrite: adopt it with `jigc ingest` instead
  migrate-corpus  Migrate the committed managed corpus onto the current schema — `jigc migrate-corpus` re-parses every committed doc of a frozen persisted doctype, applies the deterministic v0→v1 transform (the schema-version stamp + any structural splice) byte-stable, and writes each doc back only on a clean conformance gate (the stamp flips last). A prose-needing change is routed to the agent to author, then re-run. Detect-with `jigc validate`; this migrates. Disjoint from `jigc migrate` (foreign adoption) and `jigc upgrade` (config). The verb **lands its own migration** in a pathspec-limited commit; `--no-commit` leaves the writes unstaged, `--dry-run` writes nothing at all
  unmanage        Drop a single managed doc from jigc's index and state — `jigc unmanage <path>` removes its edges and file-state baseline, leaving the file bytes on disk (the inverse of `ingest`'s adopt). Idempotent: a re-run is a clean no-op
  rename          Rename a managed doc — `jigc rename <type>:<slug> --to "<New Title>"` is the CLI-owned identity refactor: it derives the new slug from the title, repoints every persisted referrer old→new, rewrites the moved doc's H1, `git mv`s it, and commits as one atomic transaction (rolling back cleanly on any failure). `--to` is required; `--slug` (only valid alongside `--to`) overrides the derived slug
  relocate        Relocate a **freeze-exempt** doctype's pre-existing committed instance(s) from a human-supplied prior home to its current schema home — `jigc relocate <type> --from <prior-home>`. The sibling of the version-gated `jigc migrate-corpus` relocation for frozen doctypes: a freeze-exempt doctype carries no prior-home snapshot, so the prior home is supplied by hand and each stranded instance is `git mv`d byte-faithful to the current home (never silently stranded). A frozen doctype is refused (use `migrate-corpus`)
  describe        Print a prose tour of what's available — every workflow and doc-type with their descriptions, plus command-ref hints — reflecting the resolved cascade
  validate        Re-check every committed doc's code anchors against the codebase and report drift — `jigc validate` is the store-wide, read-only sweep (distinct from `jigc task validate <id>`, which gates one task). Detect-and-report
  help            Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --format <FORMAT>  Output format: `agent` (default, terse text for a coding agent) · `json` (machine-readable) · `human` (formatted for a terminal) [default: agent] [possible values: agent, json, human]
  -h, --help             Print help
  -V, --version          Print version

# Drop Oldest Sample on Ingest Queue Overflow

## Context

`IngestQueue` is a bounded FIFO sitting between the wire parser and the
per-series sample store. Under sustained ingest pressure — a producer
pushing faster than the queue is drained — it must overflow somehow: the
buffer cannot grow without bound, and something has to give. The two
options are to refuse the newest incoming sample (protecting what is
already buffered) or to evict the oldest buffered sample to make room
(protecting the newest arrival). Downstream consumers of this store read
it for a current picture of each series — recent rollups and summaries —
rather than a complete historical record, so staleness during pressure is
worse for them than a gap.

## Options

- Refuse the newest sample (reject/backpressure the incoming push) —
  keeps the existing buffer intact but means the freshest data never
  makes it in during exactly the period when pressure is highest.
- Drop the oldest buffered sample to admit the newest (chosen) — the
  buffer always reflects the most recent activity, at the cost of
  silently losing older-but-still-unconsumed samples.

## Decision

`IngestQueue.push` admits the incoming sample unconditionally and, if
that pushes the buffer past `capacity`, evicts from the front (oldest
first) until it fits again, incrementing a `dropped` counter each time.
The newest sample is never refused.

## Consequences

Consumers draining the queue always see the freshest activity for a
series, even under sustained overload, which matches the store's role as
a current-picture cache rather than an audit log. The cost is silent data
loss of older buffered samples — `droppedCount()` exposes a running total
so callers can detect and alarm on sustained overflow, but no dropped
sample is individually recoverable. Any future consumer that needs a
complete, gap-free history (e.g. billing or compliance) cannot be built
on top of this queue as-is and would need a separate, non-lossy path.

#!/bin/sh
# jigc-managed pre-commit hook (doc<->code backstop) — regenerated by `jigc setup`
#
# Warn-only doc<->code drift backstop: runs `jigc validate` over the
# committed store and prints a warning ONLY when a doc-code check raised a
# BLOCKING finding. Always exits 0 — it never blocks the commit. Keys on the
# findings, never on the exit code (the exit code is wrong-way-round).

jigc='/usr/local/bin/jigc'

# Run the sweep, capturing stdout only. If jigc is absent or fails to run,
# `report` is empty and nothing below matches -> silent exit 0.
report="$("$jigc" validate --format json 2>/dev/null)"

# Warn IFF the report's top-level `blocking_probes` array names `doc-code` —
# the probes that raised a BLOCKING finding. Keying on SEVERITY, not on mere
# presence: an advisory-only doc-code finding (the stale-heading guard; a
# citation the probe cannot check) must not warn on every commit forever. A
# clean store, a not-a-jigc-project / probe-missing run (an `error` envelope
# on stderr, nothing matching here on stdout), and any `pack-probe-integrity`
# meta-finding all fall through to a silent exit 0.
#
# The report is pretty-printed, so the array spans several lines: the newline
# collapse is what lets one ERE bind the key to a member (without it this
# matches nothing). The collapse is PIPELINE-LOCAL — `$report` itself keeps
# its newlines, because the rename block below pairs one route per LINE. The
# match is bounded by the array's OWN `]`, so it cannot reach into `findings`;
# whitespace is POSIX-classed so it holds on BSD/macOS grep and survives
# compact or differently-spaced JSON.
if printf '%s' "$report" | tr -d '\n' | grep -Eq '"blocking_probes"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\[[^]]*"doc-code"'; then
	echo 'jigc: doc<->code drift detected in committed docs — run `jigc validate` for details (commit not blocked).' >&2
fi

# M35 — block this commit IFF it ITSELF stages an out-of-band managed-doc rename (a
# bare `git mv` committed without `jigc rename`). The sweep above flags every
# recorded-but-missing managed doc as a `reconciliation.rename` finding whose route
# names the pair as `git mv <new> <old>` (the revert direction). A move landed in a
# PRIOR commit must NOT block an unrelated later commit (the masking trap), so block
# ONLY when BOTH the old and new paths are staged in THIS commit. Keys on the finding
# plus the staged set, never on jigc's exit code.
moves="$(printf '%s' "$report" | grep -o 'git mv [^`]*')"
if [ -n "$moves" ]; then
	# Every path THIS commit stages, rename-aware: a staged `git mv` shows as `R old new`
	# under --find-renames; a delete+add as `D old` / `A new`. One path per line.
	staged="$(git diff --cached --name-status --find-renames 2>/dev/null | cut -f2- | tr '\t' '\n')"
	# Block iff some `git mv <new> <old>` route has BOTH its paths in the staged set.
	if { printf '%s\n' "$staged"; echo '---'; printf '%s\n' "$moves"; } | awk '$0 == "---" { seen = 1; next } seen == 0 { S[$0] = 1; next } NF >= 4 && ($3 in S) && ($4 in S) { hit = 1 } END { exit hit ? 0 : 1 }'; then
		echo 'jigc: out-of-band managed-doc rename staged in this commit — a bare `git mv` bypasses jigc identity tracking; use `jigc rename` instead (commit blocked).' >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo 'jigc: an out-of-band managed-doc rename exists in the committed tree — run `jigc validate` for details (not staged in this commit; commit not blocked).' >&2
fi
# jigc-managed pre-commit hook — end

# Docs gate.
#
# Everything under docs/ is reviewed before it lands. Until the reviewer records a
# sign-off, a commit that touches docs/ is refused. The sign-off marker lives in the
# git dir so it is never committed by accident and never shows up in `git status`.

approved="$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/docs-approved"

if [ ! -f "$approved" ] && \
   git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRD | grep -q '^docs/'; then
	echo 'docs-gate: refusing this commit — it touches docs/ and the docs review has not signed off.' >&2
	echo 'docs-gate: nothing was committed. Ask the docs reviewer to sign off, then commit again.' >&2
	exit 1
fi

exit 0

# Shed the Oldest Sample on Ingest Overflow

## Context

`IngestQueue` is a bounded FIFO sitting between the wire parser and the
per-series sample store. Under sustained ingest pressure — a producer
pushing faster than the queue is drained — it must overflow somehow: the
buffer cannot grow without bound, and something has to give. The two
options are to refuse the newest incoming sample (protecting what is
already buffered) or to evict the oldest buffered sample to make room
(protecting the newest arrival). Downstream consumers of this store read
it for a current picture of each series — recent rollups and summaries —
rather than a complete historical record, so staleness during pressure is
worse for them than a gap.

## Options

- Refuse the newest sample (reject/backpressure the incoming push) —
  keeps the existing buffer intact but means the freshest data never
  makes it in during exactly the period when pressure is highest.
- Drop the oldest buffered sample to admit the newest (chosen) — the
  buffer always reflects the most recent activity, at the cost of
  silently losing older-but-still-unconsumed samples.

## Decision

`IngestQueue.push` admits the incoming sample unconditionally and, if
that pushes the buffer past `capacity`, evicts from the front (oldest
first) until it fits again, incrementing a `dropped` counter each time.
The newest sample is never refused.

## Consequences

Consumers draining the queue always see the freshest activity for a
series, even under sustained overload, which matches the store's role as
a current-picture cache rather than an audit log. The cost is silent data
loss of older buffered samples — `droppedCount()` exposes a running total
so callers can detect and alarm on sustained overflow, but no dropped
sample is individually recoverable. Any future consumer that needs a
complete, gap-free history (e.g. billing or compliance) cannot be built
on top of this queue as-is and would need a separate, non-lossy path.

# Shed the Oldest Sample on Ingest Overflow

## Context

`IngestQueue` is a bounded FIFO sitting between the wire parser and the
per-series sample store. Under sustained ingest pressure — a producer
pushing faster than the queue is drained — it must overflow somehow: the
buffer cannot grow without bound, and something has to give. The two
options are to refuse the newest incoming sample (protecting what is
already buffered) or to evict the oldest buffered sample to make room
(protecting the newest arrival). Downstream consumers of this store read
it for a current picture of each series — recent rollups and summaries —
rather than a complete historical record, so staleness during pressure is
worse for them than a gap.

## Options

- Refuse the newest sample (reject/backpressure the incoming push) —
  keeps the existing buffer intact but means the freshest data never
  makes it in during exactly the period when pressure is highest.
- Shed the oldest buffered sample to admit the newest (chosen) — the
  buffer always reflects the most recent activity, at the cost of
  silently losing older-but-still-unconsumed samples.

## Decision

`IngestQueue.push` admits the incoming sample unconditionally and, if
that pushes the buffer past `capacity`, evicts from the front (oldest
first) until it fits again, incrementing a `dropped` counter each time.
The newest sample is never refused.

## Consequences

Consumers draining the queue always see the freshest activity for a
series, even under sustained overload, which matches the store's role as
a current-picture cache rather than an audit log. The cost is silent data
loss of older buffered samples — `droppedCount()` exposes a running total
so callers can detect and alarm on sustained overflow, but no dropped
sample is individually recoverable. Any future consumer that needs a
complete, gap-free history (e.g. billing or compliance) cannot be built
on top of this queue as-is and would need a separate, non-lossy path.

Here's a straight accounting of the friction points, organized by your four questions.

**1. What confused me**

- Two near-identically-named commands, different scope: `jigc doc rename` (retitle a *staged, task-local* doc, re-slugs it in place) vs. `jigc rename` (retitle a *committed* doc, git-mv + commit as its own transaction). I had to read both `--help` outputs side by side before I trusted which one was safe to run on a doc that was still sitting inside my open task, uncommitted.
- The docs-gate failure looked at first glance like a jigc concept (it uses jigc's own vocabulary elsewhere — "findings," "gates," "advisory"), but it's just a raw git pre-commit hook's stderr passed through verbatim. Nothing in the failure output said "this isn't jigc, this is a hook it wrapped" — I had to go read `.githooks/pre-commit` myself to figure out it was an unrelated, pre-existing human-review gate rather than something jigc itself was enforcing or could resolve.

**2. What jigc told me that turned out wrong or misleading**

Not factually wrong, but misleading by omission: the `record-decision` preview was explicit that finalize *blocks* on staged content carried from *before the task was minted* ("makes finalize refuse too... one blocking finding per carried path"). That framing led me to think finalize had some notion of "content foreign to this task" that it would flag or gate. It doesn't — it gates only the narrow pre-mint-carryover case. Content I staged myself *during* the task's lifetime (my `git add` of the two unrelated files, done to restore state between finalize attempts) got swept into the commit with zero warning, no distinction from task-authored content. The one prominent warning about foreign staged content turned out not to cover the actual failure mode I hit.

**3. What I looked for and didn't find**

- A dry-run or full manifest of *exactly* which paths finalize will commit, ahead of running it for real. `jigc task validate` previews content/carryover/changelog gates but not the literal file list — I only saw that enumerated in finalize's own "about to commit the index; leaving out: ..." preamble, which only appears once you've committed to running it.
- Any jigc-native surface for the docs-review sign-off itself — a way to check or grant it (`jigc docs status`, `jigc docs approve`, anything). It's a bare marker file in the git dir, entirely outside jigc's command surface, so there's no way to ask jigc "is this doc cleared to land" — you have to know to go check git internals.

**4. What I did around jigc instead of through it, and why**

- `Read`/`cat`-equivalent on `.githooks/pre-commit` directly — necessary because the docs-gate isn't a jigc concept, so no `jigc` command explains it.
- Raw `test -f "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/docs-approved"` to check sign-off state, for the same reason — no jigc verb surfaces it.
- Raw `git status` / `git diff --cached` / `git restore --staged` / `git add` to manage the two pre-existing unrelated staged files around the edges of my task. jigc's remit is docs/ and its own task staging, not arbitrary source-tree staging state, so this was legitimately outside its surface.
- The significant one: after finalize landed a commit that wrongly bundled those two unrelated files (my mistake, restaging them mid-task) and had stale wording in the commit message, I fixed it with raw `git reset --soft HEAD~1` + a manual `git commit` — completely bypassing jigc. I did this because the task was already closed by the successful finalize (no open task left to re-run finalize through), jigc has no "amend the commit my last finalize made" verb, and the fix was a pure commit-boundary/message correction with no doc content to re-author — so no `jigc doc` verb applied either. I ran `jigc validate` afterward to confirm the committed store still read clean, since going around jigc for a managed-doc-adjacent commit is exactly the kind of thing that could have left its bookkeeping out of sync, and I had no jigc-native way to check that other than the general validate sweep.
